entry.title: Mexico City: Days 5 to 10
entry.content:
I stayed another six nights in Hostel Mundo Joven Catedral. By my good luck, my room, 407, is the best room in the hostel. It’s on the fourth floor, spacious, has windows facing Zócalo, and there’s a table where I can working on my laptop. By my bad luck, the guy who slept on the top bunk snored so loud that it sounded like thunder for two straight nights. I couldn’t even sleep during my second night. Good thing he checked out of the hostel soon after.

I met Philip in room 407. He’s a 71 years old American Canadian who went on the walking tour with me during the first day I was at the hostel. We had a great time chatting during a buffet dinner. He’s also a minimalist and practices Vipassana meditation. We think alike on many things, such as anti-consumerism and American politics. Philip is also very soft spoken and kind. I felt he’s what I will be when I turn 71.

I also met a 47 years old Chinese woman named Dou Dou who also stayed in room 407. She’s been traveling long term and is very enthusiastic and energetic. I was impressed by the amount of sightseeing that she did.

I hung out with the 29 years old Dutch girl, Tanya, a couple of times. We strolled around in Roma Sur and La Condesa. They are neighborhoods that has a lot of expats living there. At night, I went with her, Mio, and Solal to a couple of bars in Zona Rosa. Mio is a 30 years old Japanese girl who traveled in Africa for over a year. And Solal is 29 years old and is from France.

I went to several places on my own during the day. They include Biblioteca de México “Jose Vasconcelos”, Post Palace Museum, Plaza Garibaldi, La Merced Market, Mercado Sonora, Biblioteca Vasconcelos, and Tlalpexco via the cablebus. They call it cablebus in Mexico City, but they are gondolas.

And last night was the museum night in Mexico City where many museums were free. Dou Dou, Philip, and I went to the Museum of Caricature and the Museum of the Constitutions.

I like the weather in Mexico City during this time of the year. The temperature is in the 60s and 70s F during the day, which is ideal. The metro is only MX$5, or about 25 cents USD. The cablebus is MX$7 and it’s worth it to go on for the views. However, you have to buy a MX$15 metro card to use public transit.

When I was on the cablebus to Tlalpexco I thought about how lucky I am to be traveling and to be in Mexico City. Most people are living under tin roofs or simple houses on this side of the city. For some reason, I connect with the poor more than the rich. I think I will be happier living within my means in a simple apartment than in a mansion full of stuff. There’s just something nostalgic about these simple houses. Then I remembered my childhood in Beijing, China. Even though we lived in an apartment on the third floor of an apartment building, there were some people who lived in shacks close by us. But there was always a sense of community and people helping each other. It’s nothing like the individualism in the US.

I will be checking out of Hostel Mundo Joven Catedral today because the hostel is fully booked for the upcoming Day of the Dead festival. I will be staying at Viajero CDMX Centro Hostel for the next five nights.

entry.title: Mexico City, Mexico: Days 1 to 4
entry.content:
I arrived in Mexico City International Airport Benito Juárez on the night of October 19th. I had trouble finding the public transit that goes into the city, but when I checked the price on Uber, it was only US$9 for a ride to the hostel. So I took that instead of the metro.

The first thing I noticed in Mexico City was the excessive amount of police presence. Apparently, people felt safer when there are a lot of police around. My hostel is the Hostel Mundo Joven Catedral. It’s right by Zócalo, the city center where the big church is. This hostel also has a rooftop bar where the view is fantastic!

I didn’t know what to do on the first day. I did more research on the Spanish schools. I found a school called Lengua and Cultura that I liked, but couldn’t find decent housing in the nearby La Condesa neighborhood on Airbnb. I decide it’s probably better to take a Spanish class somewhere in Guatemala instead and just enjoy being a tourist in Mexico.

As luck would have it, just when I was walking out of the hostel a tour guide named Benito asked me if I wanted to go on a guided walking tour with the people from the hostel. I decided to join so I can meet some new people.

We took the metro to Bosque de Chapultepec, a very large park with a big cemetery. Benito told us during the Day of the Dead there will be many people visiting the graves and leaving flowers on them. He also suggested that I should book my stays soon because Day of the Dead is November 1st and 2nd and there will be parades. Prices will go up by a lot since the event is very popular.

Benito took us to Museo Casa Presidencial Lázaro Cárdenas. It was the president’s house and is now a museum. Lázaro Cárdenas was a benevolent dictator who ruled Mexico for 30 years before term limits were imposed.

We also walked to Monumental Fuente de Nezahualcóyotl where Benito told us before the Aztecs there was Nezahualcóyotl, who formed alliances with two other tribes and thus forming the Aztec Triple Alliance.

I had a great time on the walking tour and met Gerardo, Mexican guy who lives in Tijuana, and Tanja, a Dutch traveler, among others.

That same night, I met Piña in my dorm room. He was born in Venezuela and worked in Miami as a massage therapist. Together with Gerardo, the three of us went to La Burra Blanca del 56, a local bar. Gerardo had me try pulque, a very light alcoholic drink made from the agave plant. I enjoyed the pineapple flavored pulque.

After Piña left, Gerardo and I walked along Madero pedestrian street for a night stroll and eating some street corns. I learned that Gerardo works as a healer. When I told him about my bipolar condition, he suggested I should try the toad venom that’s only in Mexico. Gerardo told me that there’s something called 5-MeO-DMT in the toad venom that “resets” the brain, so it can help me with bipolar. As a matter of fact, Gerardo can administer the toad venom if I meet him later at a hostel in Tepoztlán, not far from Mexico City. I was intrigued because ideally I want to find a cure for my condition.

The next morning, I did more research about 5-MeO-DMT. There have been studies done with people with depression and PTSD, but no research is done on bipolar patients because it might trigger a manic episode. If I were to try 5-MeO-DMT I would want to be in a safe setting with doctors, not at some hostel. I decided to decline Gerardo’s offer, but I might go to the hostel in Tepoztlán since it’s only about two hours away from Mexico City and at a scenic place. I’ll have to see.

The next day, I missed the 11 AM walking tour because I overslept. I ended up going to Chinatown with Piña. Benito had told me it’s the smallest Chinatown in the world because it’s only two streets, and he was right.

Back at the hostel, Piña and I chatted with Maria, a girl from Brazil. I felt Piña wanted to chat with her more so I left with Gerardo and Tanja. We went to La Burra Blanca del 56 for food then went dancing at a reggae bar called Cultural Roots. I don’t really dance because I can’t keep a beat for the life of me.

When I came back to the hostel, I saw Maria was still there. I learned about her Quimbanda religion. I was very interested because I’ve never heard about it. Apparently, a spirit from the past can possess you and help you in life. However, I was turned off by it because to be possessed by the spirit I might have to drink chicken blood or goat blood, which I find to be disgusting.

Between Gerardo and Maria, I felt I was introduced to the spiritual side of Latin America. With the Day of the Dead coming up, I felt this might be a good time to get in touch with my spirituality. It’s very interesting to learn about the toad venom and Quimbanda, but I don’t think I will try them.

Yesterday, I woke up late again and missed the walking tour. I had some delicious street tacos before going to the Estanquillo Museum. I didn’t like this museum because everything was in Spanish and I didn’t know what I was looking at. Later on, I went to Museo Nacional De Arte (MUNAL) with Tanja and Piña. We had a good time looking at some art there. The architecture inside is very cool, especially the staircase.

I have to switch rooms at the hostel because I extended until the 29th so I have to check out at 11 AM. I booked the Viajero CDMX Centro Hostel from October 29 to November 3. Benito was right about the prices. I paid close to US$500 for the five nights at Viajero. The most I’ve paid for any hostel stays.

entry.title: Miami: 5 Days
entry.content:
On October 14, I left King of Prussia and took a flight to Miami. Since I had stored all my things in the storage unit, I left the house early and had plenty of time. I decided to visit Philadelphia Chinatown before boarding the plane.

For some reason, I wanted to pray at a temple. I’m not religious, but I think it’ll help my travels if I did a little praying. More specifically, I wanted to pray to my grandma for a safe trip. My grandma was the nicest person I had ever met and she raised me until I was eleven years old. I took three bows at the Fo Shou Temple in Chinatown then had my last meal at Nan Zhou Hand Drawn Noodle House before leaving Philadelphia.

Everything was smooth at the airport and on the plane. I arrived in Miami Airport soon after the sunset and took a Lyft to Viajero Hostel, a hostel that I had stayed four years ago in Miami.

Viajero Hostel is in Miami Beach and is a block away from the beach. I ended up seeing the sunrise every morning except for one when it rained. Miami South Beach is also one of my favorite beaches in the world because of its vastness and the warm water.

The first time I was here was in the summer of 2003 when I was traveling around the United States on Greyhound buses. Now, it’s my third or fourth time here. I really like the art deco buildings as well. They remind me of the video game GTA Vice City.

The first day, I walked all the way south to South Pointe Park Pier where an retired man named Gary started chatting with me while we watched container ships going out into the sea from the port. Gary told me many interesting stories from his past, including how the SR-71 Blackbird airplane got its titanium material from the Russians, his adventures in South Africa, and his meetings with Steve Jobs when he used to work for Princeton University before he retired. Gary had such an interesting life!

The following day, I was feeling a bit bored since there’s nothing to do except for the beach. I ended up taking a stroll to Lincoln Road and Española Way. I felt a bit lonely and the hostel didn’t seem as social as four years ago. However, in my dorm room I met Yanis, a French exchange student, and Patrick, an African living in Belgium. We would spend the next day together with a German guy name Yanik.

The highlight of that day was a car trip outside of Miami Beach to Wynwood and Little Havana. Wynwood is famous for its street art. I had been there before and the place still felt a bit fake, like it was all manufactured for tourists.

In Little Havana, we had a great time eating dinner at El Rey De Las Fritas. I had to try to the famous frita sandwich. Afterward, we walked along 8th Street, the main drag of Little Havana. Yanis and Yanik bought some cigars before we came back to the hostel.

Yesterday, Sameer, my college friend from the University of Rochester, and I went to an alumni picnic event in Boca Raton’s Sugar Sand Park.

I’ve known Sameer for over 20 years. He and his wife and two kids live in the Coconut Grove neighborhood of Miami. They have a different life than mine. My life is more nomad and their life is rooted. However, I think we are the result of our decisions and choices based on our circumstances. I’m very glad Sameer was able to build his life in Miami as a real estate developer. Even though it’s been 20 years since we graduated from college we still kept in touch. It was just by luck that the university had a picnic event that day and Sameer registered for both of us to attend.

I had a good time at the picnic, but I felt I was an outlier because people wanted to know what other people’s professions are, but I don’t have one anymore. Nonetheless, I enjoyed the BBQ and met some alumni.

This morning, I saw my last sunrise at Miami Beach. My plane to Mexico City is at 5:12 PM so I have plenty of time to get to the airport. I plan to stay in Mexico City for at least a month so I can take a Spanish class. I still have to register and find an apartment.

entry.title: Last Day in KOP
entry.content:
Today is my last day in King of Prussia, PA. This afternoon, I will board a plane and fly to Miami. It’ll be a start of a new adventure.

I feel both freeing and a bit uncertain. Not having a home base means I don’t know where I’ll come back to. At the same time, I don’t have to worry about when to be back. I certainly feel lighter than before and don’t have many burdens holding me back, but the future does scare me just a little.

Over the past several days, I sorted and edited my 2025 and 2026 photographs. They are now included in my photo portfolio on this website. That’s the most important thing I accomplished recently.

From the previous post, I wrote that I will be posting some photographs of the area that I’m currently living. So here are some photos of Wayne and King of Prussia.

entry.title: Closing of a Chapter
entry.content:
A few weeks ago, my landlady terminated my lease at the house that I’m staying in King of Prussia, PA. She gave me until December 1 to move out. I was not completely surprised because there were some frictions already. It was a matter of time when I will leave the house, and ultimately King of Prussia. Though, I was hoping that I’ll leave after coming back from my Latin America travels, but it’ll be sooner than that.

I was feeling depressed for about three days. I applied to some jobs thinking that’ll be my next step. However, it’ll be the holiday season soon and there won’t be much hiring. I thought about buying my dad’s old minivan and start a vanlife. Later, I decided against that since it’ll be winter soon and the idea of a vanlife doesn’t really appeal to me right now. Then I thought, why not continue my travel adventures in Latin America. That idea seems more fun than a job or a vanlife. So I pushed my 2027 travel plan ahead of schedule and bought a plane ticket to Miami on October 14, then another ticket to Mexico City on October 19. I feel good about this decision and it gives me the excitement I need.

I plan to take a Spanish course in Mexico City, maybe for a month to start then see how I feel. After Mexico, I’ll work my way south to Central America then South America. It’ll be at least six months of solo backpacking travels in the Americas. I might apply for jobs from abroad starting early next year since the timezones are similar. I might also get a CELTA certificate in Argentina and get a position teaching English somewhere. From South America I don’t know where to go. I might come back to the States or take a direct flight to New Zealand and travel there and Australia. It’s too far away to think about in terms of a timeline, but it’ll be an adventure for sure.

Back at home, I voted by mail-in ballot for the mid-term election. Voting is important to me now than ever so I’m glad I did that. I contacted my friends and had conversations with them one last time before my departure. I also booked a storage unit to store all my things, which is just six or seven boxes. Lastly, I’m trying to sell more of my things on Facebook Marketplace and Mercari to downsize further.

I still feel bored everyday because I’m just waiting for my departure. I still take my morning walks and do some writing to pass away the time. I’m currently sorting my 2025-26 travel photos and I hope to upload them to this website before I leave. But I feel nostalgic already, thinking that the Wegmans shopping trip is my last time there, or that my next library trip will be my last, maybe I’ll attend my last hiking meetup next weekend.

I realized that it’s been ten years since I moved to the Philadelphia area for work. First, I rented a room in Blue Bell, then moved to North Wales, then West Oak Lane, then Wayne, and now King of Prussia. My time here has been great overall mainly because I was able to adapt well and make wise choices, such as going through a breakup and manage job changes. I will look back on this time period as one of my more enjoyable periods in my adult life. I hope the next ten years will be even better, wherever I will be.

During the days before my departure, I will take some photographs and post them in my next blog post to commemorate my time here.

entry.title: Europe Trip Summary
entry.content:
It’s been about a week since I came back to the US. I had a great time traveling and bike touring in Europe for four months.

First, I backpacked in Italy and Malta, then I picked up my bicycle in Wroclaw, Poland, and biked to Athens, Greece. I took trains, ferries, and a bus to get to my destination because I was tired at the end. Due to the heat dome in Europe, I had to cycle early in the morning. I only averaged about 25 miles per cycling day. In Athens, I sold my bicycle and touring gears to Rodrigo and my camping gears to Sarah.

2026 Europe bike tour map

The highlight of the bike tour was the people I met.

I was very happy to meet Henryk in Bratislava, Slovakia. He was such an interesting person and is living a life that I hope to live one day. He works whenever he wants to and goes on bike tours and hiking trips according to his own will. Henryk also gave me the advice of becoming a project manager if I want to return to a corporate life.

Additionally, I met Chuck and Susan. I consider them as the Godfather and Godmother of Warmshowers hosts. Together, they have hosted close to 1600 cyclists by the time I stayed with them in Shkoder, Albania. They also allowed me to stay for nine days, which was a very long time.

There were many other people I met on my bike tour. All of them have changed me in one way or another. I’m very grateful for this experience.

The total cost of this trip was $8745 for four months. This comes out to an average of $2186 per month, or $72.88 per day. Since I stayed in hotels, guesthouses, and hostels during the majority of my bike tour, the expenses were higher than a typical bicycle tourist. For a comparison, in 2018 I spent about $50 per day for my bike tour across the US.

I will not be bike touring for a while now that I sold my bicycle and all my camping gears in Athens. I will do a backpacking trip in Latin America as my next trip in 2027.
entry.summary: It’s been about a week since I came back to the US. I had a great time traveling and bike touring in Europe for four months.

entry.title: Days 80 to 83: Four More Days in Athens

link.title: Days 80 to 83: Four More Days in Athens

entry.content:
If someone asks me what’s the best part of Athens, the answer for me would be the people I met over the last ten days.

First there was Rodrigo, who bought my bicycle. I spent the most time with him hanging out at the hostel because the weather has been so hot during the day. He’s friends with a bunch of female travelers, Alba, Rosio, and Jenna. Together, we celebrated Rodrigo’s 38th birthday. I bought him a cake because I had told him that if I sell my bicycle before his birthday I would buy him a cake. It turned out that I sold my bike to him. Lol!

I sold my camping gears to an American girl named Sarah. She was also interested in my bike, but Rodrigo was at the hostel before her. I felt bad that I didn’t sell my bike to her and offered to treat her to lunch, but our schedule didn’t align. I hope she bought a bicycle somewhere else.

I also met up with Dale at a cafe. We had met last year in Nicosia, Cyprus. It was great catching up with her in Athens. She’s been traveling for five years and I need to learn from her on how to travel slowly.

At the Athens Hawks hostel, I had to switch to a different room. There I met Daniel, a young Brazilian guy who will try to get a job in Germany. I also met Max, a student studying business law. The three of us grabbed dinner at a gyro restaurant where the waiter didn’t think Max could finish his meal due to its large portion. After Max proved him wrong, the waiter, whose name is Dimitry, gave him a free can of Pepsi. I thought the whole thing was so funny because Max owed me a can of soda after losing a bet on the time of sunset over the mountains.

At night on the hostel rooftop bar, we caught up with our other roommates, Kacey and Catia. They are 18 and 19 years old Australian girls. I learned that Kacey’s mother is an opera singer who might have performed on the stage when my parents were living in New York City in the 90s. In fact, there was a good chance that my parents saw Kacey’s mom perform Madam Butterfly. What a small world!

I played three games of pool with two other roommates, Raf and Zoey. Raf is looking at perspective graduate schools and Zoey is almost done finishing a data science master degree from Columbia University.

Yesterday, after staying at Athens Hawks hostel for nine nights, I finally checked out and met up with Paweł, my Couchers host, near Nea Ionia district. Paweł is such an interesting person. He completed his data science master degree not too long ago and is really interested in data privacy. He’s the first person I met who has GrapheneOS installed on his phone. He showed me a bunch of resources online so I can learn more about privacy tools. Inspired by him, I made changes to my website where I removed Disqus commenting system since they were placing ads on my posts, and deleted Google Analytics in the html header so Google can’t track visitors to my website. Even though I won’t be able to see visitor information, I feel it’s a minor inconvenience for me.

Today, I met Marena and Eduardo. They are a couple who arrived at Paweł’s place and will also be staying with him for two nights. Marena is a singer and Eduardo is a saxophone player. They plan on busking at the Acropolis this afternoon to earn some money before going camping at one of the islands nearby.

I’ve thoroughly enjoyed my time in Athens even though I didn’t go to any islands near Athens. Max and I did spent a morning hiking up to Lycabettus Hill to get a good view of the city and visiting Athens National Garden.

Athens, as a city, reminded me a lot of Philadelphia. It’s gritty in certain areas, such as the neighborhood where the hostel is located. Yet other parts of the city are cleaner and geared toward tourists. I hope to be back in Athens again so I can use it as a base to explore the Greek islands. I just didn’t feel like doing any more exploring now that my bike tour has ended.

Overall, my backpacking trip to Italy and Malta has been great and my bike tour from Wrocław, Poland, to Athens, Greece, has been amazing despite the heat. Tomorrow, I will take the 1 PM flight from Athens to Philadelphia. There are so many things I want to do at home, and I will write up a trip summary when I get back.

entry.title: Days 74 to 79: Five Days in Athens

link.title: Days 74 to 79: Five Days in Athens

entry.content:
Over the past five days, I only explored Athens for two of the days. I was too worried about selling my bicycle since that’s what I decided to do.

I listed my bike on Buycycle.com and Facebook Marketplace. There was a buyer from each platform, but I ended up selling my bike, along with the panniers, repair tools and parts, some bike clothing, etc, to Rodrigo, the traveler I had met during the first day of my stay at the hostel. He decided to start his first bicycle tour and ride around Europe and maybe go to Türkiye. It’s his 38th birthday today and he sees a new adventure coming.

I was glad to have sold my bike, but I felt bad because there was a girl from Florida who had contacted on Facebook Marketplace and wanted to buy the bike, too. She was disappointed after I sold it to Rodrigo. But she might buy my camping gears and I will try to help her find another bicycle to purchase in Athens.

As for the city of Athens, I walked to Areopagus Hill to get a good view of the Acropolis, then paid €30 as the entrance fee to go inside the grounds of the Acropolis. I also saw the Parthenon and some ancient temples there.

Yesterday after selling my bike, I took a walking tour with Rodrigo and his friends, Bradley and Lucre, to Philopappos Hill to get another good view of the city. We also went to Anafiotika, a neighborhood in Athens that’s full of buildings painted white. There was also a great view from there.

For lunch, we ended up at a vegan restaurant called Mama Tierra Acropolis. The food was excellent. No wonder it has a 4.9 rating with over 1000 reviews.

At the Athens Hawks hostel, I extended my stay until the 24th. After that I will stay with a Couchers host named Paweł for two nights before getting on my flight to Philadelphia.

I’m glad I sold the bike so I don’t have to find a bike box anymore and flying will be so much easier without a bike.

entry.title: My Priority Apollo
entry.content:
Background

I purchased this bicycle from Priority Bicycles in September 2022 for a retail value of $1999, but it was $2225 in total, including shipping to a local bike shop, have it assembled professionally, and paid sales tax.

2022 Priority Apollo webpage

I used this bicycle for two bike tours. One is from King of Prussia, PA, to Gainesville, FL, in 2023 (1968 miles). The other is from King of Prussia, PA, to Athens, Greece, in 2025-26 (5485 miles). The total odometer mileage is about 7500 miles, or ~12000 km.

I gave this bike the name: Serendipity.

Maintenance

This bicycle has been great and lives up to the low maintenance reputation that Priority advertises. Once I installed Schwalbe Marathon Almotion tubeless tires, I had no flats during my Europe bike tour.

The bike is very quiet when ridden, the gears can be changed when the bike is stopped, and the ride is very smooth. Moreover, during rainy days, the bike doesn’t need its chain to be lubed because it doesn’t have a chain, but a belt. You basically get a free bike wash when it rains.

Here’s some more detailed information about the various components and maintenance videos:

Component Maintenance/Info
Shimano Alfine SG-S7001-11 hub - Oil should be changed every 5000 km
- Use only Shimano SG-S700 oil
- Video: How to change the oil
- PDF: Alfine 11 Hub service manual (oil change instruction starts on page 23)
Gates carbon belt 118 CDX - Can last 30000 km
- Video: How to safely coil a belt
- Video: Belt tension adjustment
- Video: Changing the belt
- Video: Apollo gear adjustment
Bottom bracket 68mm GXP
Spokes - Front wheel: 294mm/ 14G
- Rear wheel: 270mm/ 14G
Rim tape size 28 mm X 11 m WTB TCS
Schwalbe Marathon Almotion (Tubeless) tires - Size: 40-622; 28x1.50; 700x38C
- Pressure: 3.5-5.5 bar (50-70 psi)
- Last between 6000 and 10000 km
- Video: Seal a punctured tire
- Video: Rear flat tire repair
- Video: Remove and install a tire and tube
- Video: Patch an inner tube
Widest tire width 45 mm
Narrowest tire width 28 mm

Conclusion

I hope the next owner can take good care of this bicycle. I enjoyed riding this bike a lot. It’s been a great bike!

Contact

For any questions regarding this bike, you can contact me via the About page. You can also email Priority Bicycles directly. Their customer service is top notch!

Cycling Resources

For more cycling resources and tips, I wrote up this resource guide on my old blog.

entry.title: Days 72 and 73: Ferry from Corfu to Igoumenitsa, then Bus to Athens

link.title: Days 72 and 73: Ferry from Corfu to Igoumenitsa, then Bus to Athens

entry.content:
Two days ago, I took the 9 AM ferry from Corfu to Igoumenitsa. The ferry ride was about 1:30 hours and it was very scenic with the mountains on both sides.

I stayed at Hotel Astoria in Igoumenitsa, which is very close to the ferry terminal. I didn’t do much in town except for getting some meals. Igoumenitsa seems to be just a place for the ferry with nothing special about it.

The next morning, I went to the bus station and spent €68.20 for a bus ticket to Athens. The price included a €15 fee for the bicycle.

The bus ride was from 8:30 AM to about 4 PM. It was a long ride, but I enjoyed the beautiful mountain scenery while listened to some music.

Once I reached the bus station in Athens, I rode about two miles to Athens Hawks hostel. I was glad that I could store my bicycle in the basement of the hostel.

This hostel is a nice hostel. The rooms are clean and there’s a social area. I met another traveler named Rodrigo in the afternoon. He’s from Uruguay. We went to a Pakistani restaurant near the hostel for dinner then walked around the neighborhood for a little while. It seems I’m in a neighborhood full of immigrants.

I only booked for two nights at the hostel, most likely I will extend a few more nights at least. I need to acquire a cardboard bicycle box, but right now there’s a holiday in Greece. From the WhatsApp Europe Cycling group, I read that most bike shops in Athens are closed due to the holiday. I will have to wait a few days then contact the shops. Meanwhile, I plan to do laundry one last time and explore Athens.
